title: Cap. 4 Mem. 1 Rat. 3: Sufficient for humans as denied for fallen angels — objection and reply
pass_a_gloss: Rat.3: Christ sufficienter dead for all humans in the sense denied for fallen angels — confessed by orthodox. Ambrose on Ps 118: mystical Sun of righteousness rose/came/suffered/rose for all; unbeliever defrauds himself of general benefit; why not ‘mercy fills heaven’? spiritual wickedness in heavenlies don’t share common jus indulgentiae/remission. So all humans have common right to obtain pardon by faith; demons don’t, because Christ never died for them. Even restrictivists grant: not same ratio for any humans as for diaboli re death’s sufficiency — lytron apt for humans if they will embrace, not for diaboli. Observation: paid so diaboli cannot be redeemed even if supposed to believe (not paid for them); exhibited so any humans can be if they will believe — because offered/paid for all of them. Without ordinata (only mera from intrinsic value), no discrimen vs daemons for Ambrose’s jus indulgentiae. Passion’s value from dignity of suffering Person → infinite even vs angels’ sins. Therefore humans need ordinata (Christ referring passion to all humans, not angels). Thus truly sufficienter for all humans by sufficiency that has no place vs apostate angels. Obj: mere sufficiency works for humans not diaboli because sufficiency requires aptum/idoneum — aptitude largely from assuming likeness of sinful flesh; no angelic nature assumed → not idoneous/sufficient for angels’ sins. Sol: limps both ways. (1) Mere sufficiency + any aptitude still without ordination/act of offering related to persons ≠ ‘suffered for them’ at all, let alone sufficiently — so nature-assumption doesn’t get elect-only advocates to ‘died for all humans.’ (2) Nature-dissimilarity doesn’t stop God’s blood being sufficientissimum in itself for angels’ sins too; infinite value from Divine Person. God willed to pity humans not angels; Redeemer assumed Abraham’s seed not angelic nature → conclude death not lytron ordinatum for angels’ redemption, NOT that it lacks intrinsic sufficient dignity if such ordination had been. Contrariwise Christ sufficient Head to influence grace even to good angels (theologians). That merits don’t profit bad angels → will of God alone. Hence if many humans to whom passion is in no way ordained, their condition re death’s sufficiency = Diabolorum.
pass_b_english: 3. Christ is acknowledged to have died sufficiently for all human beings in that sense in which he is denied to have died for the fallen angels. This is clear and confessed among all the orthodox, who often recall this discrimination between evil angels and any evil human beings, at least while they are wayfarers. To this look those words of Ambrose on that text of Psalm 118, The earth is full of the Lord’s mercy, Sermon 8: That mystical Sun of righteousness has risen for all, come for all, suffered for all, risen for all. But if anyone does not believe in Christ, he defrauds himself of the general benefit. A little later: Perhaps you may say, Why was it not said, THE HEAVEN IS FULL OF THE LORD’S MERCY? Because there are also spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places, but those do not pertain to the common right of God’s indulgence and the remission of sins. From which it is plain that Christ so suffered for the whole human race that all human beings thence have a common right of obtaining indulgence by faith, which the demons do not have, because he in no way died for them. Certain of our own, who fight hard for restricting Christ’s death, yet freely grant this: that there is not the same ratio for any human beings that there is for the diaboli, as to the sufficiency of Christ’s death. For to any human beings, but not to the diaboli, he paid a lytron apt enough, if only they were willing to embrace it. This discrimination in the payment of this lytron is worth observing: It was so paid to God that it cannot redeem the diaboli, even if they are supposed to believe — namely because it was not paid for them; but it was so exhibited and given to God that it can redeem any human beings, if they are willing to believe; whence this, unless because it was offered and paid for all of them? For it would not avail to free any human beings, even if they believed, unless it is supposed to have been given and offered to God for them, in the common cause of the human race, even when they did not believe. This discrimination between the sufficiency of Christ’s death as to human beings and as to demons being established — that Christ’s death is understood as sufficient for all human beings in that sense in which it is rightly denied for the angels — let us pass from this Major proposition to the minor. I say, then, that if we acknowledge no other sufficiency in Christ’s death for redeeming any human beings than that which we have called mere sufficiency, which depends on the intrinsic value of the lutron, the offerer’s ordination to persons being removed, no discrimination is set up between such persons and the demons themselves as to that right of obtaining indulgence and remission by the benefit of this lutron, which was recalled above from Ambrose and granted universally to human beings, excluded from angels. It is plain; because the value of Christ’s passion is estimated from the dignity of the suffering Person. It had therefore in itself and in its intrinsic price not only sufficiency but infinite superabundance, even if against it are weighed the sins not only of all human beings but of angels. There must therefore be granted, with respect to human beings, not only that mere sufficiency which depends on the inherent dignity of the thing offered, but that ordained one which arises from Christ’s mind and act referring this his passion to all human beings, not referring it to angels. This being posited, Christ is truly said to have died sufficiently for all human beings, by that sufficiency which has no place in relation to the apostate angels, and of which it is truly said, Christ died for the fallen angels neither efficaciously nor sufficiently.

Objection. But perhaps someone may meet this argument and assert that a mere sufficiency of the thing offered, considered in itself, as to human beings makes it that Christ is rightly said to have suffered sufficiently for all human beings; yet does not make it as to the Diaboli, because that is not sufficient which is not apt and suitable. But a great part of the aptitude in Christ for taking away human sins was that he assumed the likeness of sinful flesh. Since therefore he did not assume the nature of angels, he had neither a suitable state nor a sufficient passion for taking away the sins of evil angels. Solution. But this subtlety limps on both sides. For that mere sufficiency, even with aptitude and congruence however great added, if some ordination and action of offering related to persons has not accompanied it, does not yet make it that Christ is said to have suffered at all for such persons, much less that he is affirmed to have suffered sufficiently. In vain, then, is the assumption of human nature urged, so that from it those who contend he died for the elect alone may deduce that Christ died for all human beings, whether sufficiently or insufficiently. On the other side also the aforesaid exception wavers, because although between Christ and the Angels there did not intervene that likeness of nature which is between Christ and human beings, yet this cannot hinder the lytron paid by Christ — that is, the blood of God — from having been in itself and in its value most sufficient for taking away even the sins of angels. For what crime of any creature can be so great that the poured blood of God would not suffice to expiate it? — which has infinite value from the dignity of the Divine Person, and therefore, the dissimilarity of human nature notwithstanding, if God had deigned to indulge the angels this right in Christ’s passion, it would be applicable even to redeeming angels. God indeed willed to pity the human race, not to pity the angels; he willed the Redeemer to assume not an angelic nature but the seed of Abraham: From this we can conclude that Christ’s death is not a lytron ordained for the redemption of angels, but we neither can nor ought to conclude that it is not a lytron of sufficient dignity, value, and efficacy in itself, if that ordination had been. An argument can be made the other way: that Christ, nature’s dissimilarity notwithstanding, is a sufficient and suitable Head for pouring grace even into the angels themselves; whence the most learned Theologians assert that he merited gifts of grace and glory for the good angels themselves. But that Christ’s merits do not profit the evil angels is to be referred not to insufficiency of the thing but to the will of God alone: and consequently, if we posit many human beings to whom Christ’s passion and merit are in no way ordained, their ratio and condition as to the sufficiency of Christ’s death will be no other than that of the Diaboli.

3. Christus pro omnibus hominibus eo sensu sufficienter mortuus agnoscitur, quo pro angelis lapsis mortuus negatur. Hoc clarum est et in confesso apud omnes orthodoxos, qui saepe hoc discrimen commemorant inter angelos malos et quosvis homines malos, saltem dum viatores sunt. Huc spectant illa verba Ambrosii, in illud Psalm. cxviii. Misericordia Domini plena est terra, Serm. 8: Mysticus Sol ille justitiae omnibus ortus est, omnibus venit, omnibus passus, omnibus resurrexit. Si quis autem non credit in Christum, a generali beneficio ipse se fraudat. Paulo post, Fortasse dicas, Qua ratione non dictum sit, MISERICORDIA DOMINI PLENUM EST COELUM? Quia sunt etiam spirituales nequitiae in caelestibus, sed non illae ad commune jus indulgentiae Dei remissionemque pertinent peccatorum. Ex quibus patet, Christum ita passum pro universo humano genere, ut omnes homines inde habeant commune jus indulgentiae obtinendae per fidem, quod daemones non habent, quia pro illis nullatenus mortuus est. Quidam ex nostris, qui pro restringenda Christi morte acriter depugnant, tamen hoc ultro largiuntur, Non esse eandem rationem hominum quorumcunque quae est diabolorum, quoad sufficientiam mortis Christi. Hominibus enim quibuscunque, non autem diabolis, satis idoneum solvebat lytron, si modo amplecti vellent. Dignum est observatione hoc discrimen in hujus lytri solutione: Ita Deo persolutum est ut diabolos non possit redimere, etiamsi supponantur credere; nempe quia pro illis non fuit persolutum: at ita Deo exhibitum et datum est ut quosvis homines possit redimere, si velint credere; unde hoc, nisi quia pro illis omnibus fuit oblatum et persolutum? Non enim valeret ad homines quoscunque liberandos, etiamsi crederent, nisi supponatur pro eisdem datum et oblatum Deo, in communi causa generis humani, etiam quando non credebant. Stabilito igitur hoc discrimine inter sufficientiam mortis Christi quoad homines et quoad daemones, quod Christi mors scilicet pro omnibus hominibus eo sensu sufficiens intelligitur quo pro angelis recte negatur, ab hac Majore propositione transeamus ad minorem. Dico igitur, si aliam sufficientiam in morte Christi quoad homines quoscunque redimendos non agnoscamus, nisi eam quam appellavimus sufficientiam meram, quaeque pendet ex intrinseco valore lutri, sublata ordinatione offerentis ad personas, nullum discrimen constitui inter tales personas et ipsos daemones quoad illud jus indulgentiae et remissionis obtinendae beneficio hujus lutri, quod ab Ambrosio supra commemoratum fuit, atque hominibus universim concessum, angelis exclusum. Patet; Quia valor passionis Christi aestimatur ex dignitate personae patientis. Habuit igitur in se et intrinseco suo pretio non modo sufficientiam, sed infinitam superabundantiam, etiamsi contra appendantur peccata non hominum modo universorum, sed angelorum. Danda est ergo respectu hominum, non modo sufficientia illa mera, quae pendet ex rei oblatae insita dignitate, sed illa ordinata, quae oritur ex animo et actu Christi ad omnes homines hanc suam passionem referentis, ad angelos non referentis. Hoc posito, Christus revera dicitur pro omnibus hominibus mortuus sufficienter, illa sufficientia quae in relatione ad angelos apostatas locum non habet, et de qua vere dicatur, Christus pro angelis lapsis neque efficaciter, neque sufficienter mortuus est.

Objicitur. Sed huic argumento occurat fortasse aliquis, atque asserat, Meram rei oblatae sufficientiam in se consideratam quoad homines efficere ut Christus recte dicatur passus pro omnibus hominibus sufficienter; non tamen efficere quoad Diabolos, quia sufficiens non est quod non est aptum, idoneum. Aptitudinis autem in Christo ad peccata humana tollenda pars magna fuit, quod similitudinem carnis peccatricis assumpsit. Cum igitur angelorum naturam non assumpserit, nec statum habuit idoneum, nec sufficientem passionem ad malorum angelorum tollenda peccata.

Solutio. Sed utrinque claudicat haec argutatio. Nam sufficientia illa mera, accedente aptitudine et congruentia quantalibet, si non accesserit ordinatio aliqua et actio offerendi ad personas relata, nondum efficit ut pro talibus personis Christus passus omnino dicatur, nedum ut passus sufficienter affirmetur. Frustra igitur obtenditur humanae naturae assumptio, ut inde deducatur Christum pro omnibus hominibus fuisse mortuum sive sufficienter sive insufficienter, ab iis qui pro solis electis illum fuisse mortuum contendunt. Ex altera etiam parte vacillat praedicta exceptio, quia licet inter Christum et Angelos non intercesserit ea naturae similitudo quae inter Christum et homines, tamen hoc impedire non potest quin lytron a Christo persolutum, hoc est, sanguis Dei, fuerit in se et valore suo sufficientissimum ad tollenda etiam peccata angelorum. Quod enim potest esse tantum crimen cujuscunque creaturae, cui expiando non sufficiat effusus sanguis Dei; qui valorem habet ex dignitate Divinae personae infinitum, ac proinde non obstante humanae naturae dissimilitudine, si Deus hoc jus in passionem Christi angelis indulgere dignatus esset, etiam ad angelos redimendos applicabilem. Voluit quidem Deus humani generis misereri, angelorum non misereri; voluit Redemtorem assumere non naturam angelicam, sed semen Abrahae: Hinc concludere possumus mortem Christi non esse lytron ordinatum pro redemtione angelorum, at non esse lytron in se sufficientis dignitatis, valoris et efficacitatis, si ordinatio haec fuisset, nec possumus concludere, nec debemus. Argumentum esse potest in contrariam partem, quod Christus, non obstante naturae dissimilitudine, est sufficiens et idoneum Caput ad influendam gratiam etiam angelis ipsis; unde dona gratiae et gloriae ipsis bonis angelis meruisse a Theologis doctissimis asseritur. Quod autem malis angelis non prosunt Christi merita, id non ad insufficientiam rei, sed ad solam voluntatem Dei est referendum: ac per consequens, si ponamus homines multos, ad quos passio et meritum Christi nullatenus ordinetur, quoad sufficientiam mortis Christi non alia erit horum ratio et conditio quam Diabolorum.
